claims.text: Conventionally solidified Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 contains multiple primary non-eutectic phases.
Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 exhibits a multistep crystallization sequence.
A brief reheat-quench cycle will suppress nucleation of primary crystalline phases in the as-solidified alloy.
The reheat-quench cycle will promote amorphous retention and enhance thermal stability.
The treatment should reheat the alloy to just above its glass-transition temperature but below the onset of rapid crystallization.
The intervention can be applied after either rapid or slower initial cooling.
A very short dwell time will avoid triggering additional crystalline nucleation.
Transient reheating will increase atomic mobility enough to relieve local stresses and homogenize the supercooled liquid.
Thermal exposure can modify local atomic ordering or structural heterogeneity in a high-entropy alloy.
The brief exposure will not provide enough time for extensive crystalline nucleation and will therefore preserve an amorphous or low-crystallinity structure.
Rapidly traversing the critical nucleation-temperature window limits the time available for primary crystallization.
The subsequent quench freezes in the disordered state.
Reducing structural heterogeneity and freezing in disorder will increase the thermal stability of the amorphous phase.
Treated specimens will retain a higher amorphous-phase fraction than specimens subjected only to standard rapid or slow cooling.
Treated specimens will exhibit an upward shift in crystallization-onset temperature.
Conventional rapid or slower cooling followed by standard reheating produces extensive primary crystallization, limited amorphous content, and relatively low thermal stability in this alloy.
Excessive dwell time or reheating above the crystallization onset will promote further crystallization.

contradictions.description: The starting material is described as already containing multiple primary crystalline phases, yet a sub-crystallization-temperature reheat is proposed to suppress their nucleation and preserve a supercooled-liquid structure. Preventing new nucleation does not explain how already formed primary phases would be removed or converted into amorphous material.

The treatment is claimed to work even after slower cooling that yields extensive primary crystallization, while the proposed mediator assumes a sufficiently amorphous supercooled liquid that can be homogenized and frozen in. The necessary amorphous precursor state is not established for the slow-cooled condition.
